paragraphs: Internet congestion control decides how quickly traffic sources should transmit data so that available network capacity is used efficiently. This paper treats that decision as a reinforcement learning problem. Instead of relying solely on a predefined control procedure, it trains a deep neural network policy to respond to traffic patterns and changing network conditions.

The central finding is that learned policies can capture intricate relationships in those conditions and use them to outperform the state of the art in the authors’ investigation. This makes congestion control an application in which reinforcement learning can contribute to a core networking function, with relevance to services such as live video and connected devices.

The paper also identifies fairness, safety, and generalization as substantial obstacles to real-world adoption. Its performance results therefore accompany an explicit account of unresolved deployment challenges. To support reproducibility and further investigation, the authors provide a congestion-control test suite using the OpenAI Gym interface.
icml-2019-a-deep-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: Deep reinforcement learning improves congestion control in the authors’ investigation, while fairness, safety, and generalization remain deployment challenges.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, the information relevant to one agent can depend on what the others are doing. This paper introduces an actor-critic algorithm that trains decentralized policies with centrally computed critics. The policies govern agents’ behavior, while the critics provide evaluations used during learning.

The critics share an attention mechanism that selects relevant information separately for each agent at every timestep. This lets the training process adapt its focus as interactions change. The authors report that this selective use of information supports more effective and scalable learning in complex multi-agent environments compared with recent approaches.

The framework accommodates several different relationships between agents: they may share rewards, receive individual rewards, or operate adversarially. It also applies when no global state is supplied and imposes no assumptions on agents’ action spaces. These properties broaden its applicability beyond a single cooperative setup. The main contribution is a flexible way to coordinate training information while still learning decentralized policies.
icml-2019-actor-attention-critic-for-mul.tldr: Attention-based centralized critics help train decentralized agents by selecting relevant information for each agent at each timestep.

paragraphs: A model is often trained using one objective but judged using another. The training loss is usually chosen in advance as a convenient proxy for the evaluation metric. This paper questions whether keeping that proxy fixed is the best way to obtain the performance that actually matters.

The proposed approach meta-learns a loss function that changes during training. A sample-efficient reinforcement learning method controls this adaptation, with the evaluation metric serving as the target of optimization. This makes the design of the training objective part of the learning process itself, rather than treating it as a settled choice made before training begins.

Experiments in classification and metric learning show considerable improvements over the state of the art across the evaluated tasks. The authors associate these gains with both better metric optimization and a smoother loss landscape. They also report that learned policies transfer across tasks and data, supporting the method’s usefulness across a broad range of losses and evaluation metrics.
icml-2019-addressing-the-loss-metric-mis.tldr: Adaptive Loss Alignment learns to change the training loss so that optimization better serves the evaluation metric.

paragraphs: Time series can change their statistical behavior over time, making both causal discovery and forecasting difficult. This paper studies those two problems together using a particular nonlinear state-space model. Its central idea is that changes in the data can supply information about causal relationships as well as complicate prediction.

The model allows both the strength of causal relationships and the variance of noise to vary. Within this modeling framework, the authors show that these changes make the causal structure and model parameters identifiable. In other words, the model can distinguish the underlying causal explanation and its parameters. This is a result about the proposed framework, rather than a claim that any changing time series reveals its causes.

After learning the causal model, the method frames forecasting as Bayesian inference within it. Predictions exploit time variation and adapt as new observations arrive. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach, connecting the causal identification result to a practical method for forecasting in changing environments.
icml-2019-causal-discovery-and-forecasti.tldr: A nonlinear state-space framework uses changing causal strengths and noise variances to identify causal models and support adaptive forecasting.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether an intervention’s effect can be calculated from observational data together with knowledge about causal relationships. Many approaches assume that this knowledge specifies one complete causal diagram. This paper instead allows uncertainty over the diagram, represented by a partial ancestral graph, or PAG, that describes an equivalence class of causal diagrams.

This representation matters because a scientist need not commit to one uniquely specified diagram, and a PAG can be learned from data. Earlier conditions could establish identification in some cases but did not resolve every case. The paper supplies a complete identification algorithm for the information represented by a PAG.

Completeness gives both possible outcomes a precise meaning. If the effect is identifiable, the algorithm returns a valid expression for calculating it. If it reports failure, the effect is provably not identifiable from the available information. The authors also characterize non-identifiability graphically, providing a structural account of when this uncertainty prevents recovery of a causal effect.
icml-2019-causal-identification-under-ma.tldr: A complete algorithm determines whether a causal effect is identifiable when causal knowledge specifies a PAG rather than one diagram.

paragraphs: A complementary label tells a learner one class that an example does not belong to, without naming its true class. This paper develops a framework for training classifiers using that form of supervision. The challenge is to evaluate and improve ordinary classification performance when each training label only rules out one possibility.

The main contribution is an unbiased estimator of classification risk that supports arbitrary losses and models within the proposed framework. Its flexibility includes linear and nonlinear models as well as convex and nonconvex loss functions. This removes restrictions that had prevented earlier methods from achieving the same combination of an unbiased risk estimate and broad modeling choices.

The estimator also enables cross-validation for choosing models and hyperparameters without ordinarily labeled validation data. That extends the usefulness of complementary labels beyond fitting a classifier to selecting how it should be trained. The authors further improve the estimator using a non-negative correction and a gradient-ascent technique, and experiments demonstrate the improved approach’s superiority.
icml-2019-complementary-label-learning-f.tldr: An unbiased classification-risk estimator enables flexible training and model selection using labels that only specify an incorrect class.

paragraphs: Reusing previously learned skills could make reinforcement learning more data-efficient on new tasks. This paper examines methods that combine behaviors through their action-value functions. The authors identify situations in which two existing approaches perform poorly, showing that combining learned value information can require additional correction.

Their analysis extends a generalized policy-improvement result to the maximum-entropy framework. It also produces an algorithm for implementing successor features in continuous action spaces. These contributions support the broader goal of transferring behavior across tasks while accommodating the policy framework and action spaces considered in the paper.

The proposed composition method explicitly learns the discounted future divergence between the base policies. This quantity captures differences between their behavior and supplies a correction that addresses the identified failure cases. The method can, in principle, recover the optimal policy during transfer. Evaluations in tabular settings and continuous-control problems with compositional structure show performance that matches or exceeds existing methods on every task considered.
icml-2019-composing-entropic-policies-us.tldr: Learning future divergence between base policies corrects skill composition and can, in principle, recover an optimal transfer policy.

paragraphs: DBSCAN groups data using local density, but computing empirical density for every sample gives it quadratic worst-case running time. That cost can make large datasets difficult to process. DBSCAN++ changes this part of the procedure by evaluating densities only at a chosen subset of points.

The paper investigates how much computation this selective evaluation can save while preserving statistical quality. Its consistency guarantees describe a tradeoff between computational cost and estimation rates. Up to a certain reduction in computation, the method retains the same estimation rates. The resulting sub-quadratic algorithm attains minimax-optimal rates for level-set estimation, the statistical problem of recovering regions above a density threshold.

Empirically, DBSCAN++ achieves competitive clustering performance while using a fraction of traditional DBSCAN’s runtime. It also shows greater robustness to the bandwidth hyperparameter. Together, these findings indicate that evaluating every point’s density is not always required to retain strong results, while the theoretical tradeoff specifies that computational savings without a rate penalty have a limit.
icml-2019-dbscan-towards-fast-and-scalab.tldr: DBSCAN++ evaluates densities at selected points, reducing computation while preserving optimal estimation rates up to a stated tradeoff.

paragraphs: Network communities need not form disjoint groups: an entity can belong to several communities at once. This paper uses a mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel to represent such networks and studies when memberships of a subset of nodes can be uniquely recovered. Its focus includes settings without pure nodes that belong exclusively to one community.

The method first constructs a second-order graph moment, a summary of network relationships. As network size increases, this summary converges to a particular product of the underlying model parameters. The authors then use ideas from convex geometry to formulate an optimization problem for recovering the membership parameters from that structure.

The recovery guarantee depends on a sufficiently scattered condition on the true memberships. When that condition holds, solving the proposed problem identifies the ground truth. The authors also introduce an efficient community-detection algorithm, reporting faster operation and better convergence properties than prior work. Experiments on synthetic and real networks support the learning framework and complement its conditional identification result.
icml-2019-detecting-overlapping-and-corr.tldr: A graph-moment and geometric optimization approach identifies overlapping community memberships under a sufficiently scattered condition.

paragraphs: Predictive models may need to satisfy fairness requirements involving sensitive attributes even when access to those attributes is restricted. This paper studies fair learning under differential privacy, bringing fairness, predictive accuracy, and privacy into the same design problem. It asks how satisfying all three changes the choices available to a learning algorithm.

The first proposed algorithm privately implements an equalized-odds post-processing method. It is relatively simple, but it must explicitly use protected group membership when making predictions. The second privately adapts an oracle-efficient in-processing method. This alternative is more complex, but it does not require protected group membership at test time.

That distinction becomes central to the paper’s findings. The authors identify tradeoffs that emerge when fairness, accuracy, and privacy are required together, and show that these tradeoffs can be milder when group membership is available at prediction time. A brief experimental evaluation accompanies the analysis. The contribution therefore includes both private algorithms and an explanation of how prediction-time access to sensitive information affects their tradeoffs.
icml-2019-differentially-private-fair-le.tldr: Two private fair-learning algorithms reveal tradeoffs among fairness, accuracy, and privacy that depend on test-time access to group membership.

paragraphs: This paper improves stochastic ADMM for nonconvex optimization by incorporating the SPIDER estimator. The resulting method, SPIDER-ADMM, is designed to reach an approximate solution with fewer incremental first-order oracle calls. This complexity measure counts the gradient-information requests needed by the optimization procedure, making the theoretical comparison about computational work required to reach a specified accuracy.

The authors also develop a new analysis framework for nonconvex stochastic ADMM. Beyond analyzing their own method, they use it to establish optimal oracle-complexity results for existing SVRG-ADMM and SAGA-ADMM methods, resolving a previously unsettled question. They report that SPIDER-ADMM improves on existing stochastic ADMM methods and achieves record-setting oracle complexity for an epsilon-approximate solution.

The work extends the method to an online setting and derives an oracle-complexity result for that version as well. Benchmark experiments show faster convergence than existing ADMM algorithms for nonconvex optimization. The contribution combines a new optimizer, a reusable theoretical framework, and empirical support for the proposed methods’ convergence advantage.
icml-2019-faster-stochastic-alternating-.tldr: SPIDER-ADMM improves nonconvex stochastic optimization efficiency and introduces an analysis framework for oracle-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: A musical score contains relationships that a simple sequence can obscure. Several notes may sound simultaneously, and each note has its own duration. This paper represents score information with a graph neural network and uses that representation to generate expressive piano performances from written music.

The architecture combines a gated graph neural network at the note level with a hierarchical attention network at the measure level. It also incorporates bidirectional long short-term memory and iterative feedback. These components provide ways to process both individual notes and larger musical groupings. A variational autoencoder allows the model to represent different performance styles for the same input score.

In a listening test, the proposed model generated performances judged more human-like than those from a baseline model and a hierarchical attention model that treated the score as a word-like sequence. This result supports the value of explicitly representing the distinctive structure of musical notation. The evidence concerns perceived performance quality in the reported comparison.
icml-2019-graph-neural-network-for-music.tldr: A graph-based score model produces piano performances judged more human-like than the compared sequence-based approaches.

paragraphs: Real-world classification data can have missing values, uneven class frequencies, and missing labels at the same time. Each problem can weaken a classifier, yet preprocessing methods often address them separately. HexaGAN is a generative adversarial framework designed to handle all three together through a shared perspective.

The framework contains six interacting components and loss functions designed for that architecture. Their joint operation supports both filling in missing values and generating data conditioned on class. The approach matters because it treats the three data problems as connected parts of one learning task, rather than assuming the other problems have already been resolved.

The authors report state-of-the-art imputation performance, with improvements of up to 14%, alongside high-quality class-conditional generation. In classification experiments with 20% missingness, they report F1-score improvements of up to 5% over combinations of state-of-the-art methods. These are reported upper-end improvements in the evaluated settings, supporting the promise of jointly addressing imperfect data within a single framework.
icml-2019-hexagan-generative-adversarial.tldr: HexaGAN jointly handles missing values, class imbalance, and missing labels, improving imputation and classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Importance-weighted variational inference uses multiple independent samples to obtain a tighter lower bound on its objective. This paper explores whether coordinating those samples can reduce redundancy. It introduces a hierarchical proposal structure that makes samples dependent, with the aim of letting their contributions compensate for one another’s errors.

The intended benefit is a lower-variance importance estimator: repeated estimates would fluctuate less. The theoretical analysis examines the condition under which convergence of this variance can be connected to convergence of the lower bound. This makes the relationship between the training objective and estimator quality an explicit subject of analysis, rather than assuming they always improve together.

Empirically, maximizing the lower bound also reduces estimator variance. Further analysis attributes this effect to negative correlation introduced by the hierarchical sampling scheme, consistent with the proposed idea of compensating sample contributions. Inference performance also improves as the sample count increases. The results support coordinated sampling as a useful extension of importance-weighted inference.
icml-2019-hierarchical-importance-weight.tldr: Hierarchical proposals coordinate importance samples, with observed negative correlation reducing estimator variance and improving inference.

paragraphs: The ladder capsule network changes how a capsule architecture selects information and learns relationships between parts and wholes. It replaces the usual dynamic-routing building block with a design motivated by retaining important capsules during training. A pruning layer removes irrelevant capsules before the selected ones are used to construct higher-level capsule outputs.

A second component, the ladder layer, reconstructs lower-level capsule outputs from higher-level capsules. Training uses a reconstruction loss and backpropagation to learn this relationship. The direction is significant: higher-level representations must account for the lower-level outputs from which they were constructed, providing a reverse-direction mechanism for learning part-whole spatial relationships.

Experiments on MNIST show that the architecture learns an equivariant representation, meaning its representation changes in a corresponding way when pose changes. The authors also report better extrapolation or generalization to pose variations. These findings support the proposed combination of capsule selection and reconstruction as an alternative way to learn spatial structure in the evaluated setting.
icml-2019-ladder-capsule-network-4f3f8c7.tldr: Pruning and top-down reconstruction replace dynamic routing in a capsule network, improving pose generalization on MNIST.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks to infer a reward from observed behavior. This paper introduces a setting in which the observed agent is still learning and is therefore suboptimal. The observer uses changes in that agent’s behavior as evidence, with the explicit assumption that the observed policy improves over time.

The goal is to recover the environment’s actual reward and then use it to learn behavior that can outperform the observed agent. The authors propose practical methods based on entropy-regularized policy iteration and discuss approaches that use only trajectories through states and actions. The informative signal is thus the learner’s progression, rather than a requirement to observe an already optimal policy.

The methods are evaluated by observing agents that use various reinforcement learning algorithms. On tasks with both discrete and continuous states or actions, an observer optimizing the recovered reward can surpass the observed learner’s performance. These results demonstrate that an improving but imperfect agent can provide useful supervision for learning a stronger policy.
icml-2019-learning-from-a-learner-62f29f.tldr: An observer can infer rewards from an improving, suboptimal learner and sometimes learn a policy that surpasses it.

paragraphs: Decision-making models often assume an agent already knows every possible state and action. This paper studies a more open-ended situation: an agent may initially be unaware of actions or belief variables that are essential for success. Learning must therefore expand the agent’s understanding of the decision problem as well as improve its choices.

The proposed method learns Bayesian Decision Networks using both exploration of the domain and assertions supplied by an expert. These two sources let the agent acquire information through experience and guidance. The framework guarantees convergence to optimal behavior even when the initial representation omits critical actions or belief variables.

Experiments show the agent learning optimal behavior on both small and large decision problems. They also examine what happens when new discoveries alter its understanding of the task. Allowing the agent to preserve information it has already acquired produces faster convergence. This finding makes information retention a consequential part of learning under unawareness: expanding a model need not discard all earlier progress.
icml-2019-learning-structured-decision-p.tldr: An agent learns decision networks through exploration and expert guidance, converging to optimal behavior despite initially unknown actions or variables.

paragraphs: Transfer learning can help when a target task has little training data, but configuring transfer becomes difficult when source and target networks have different architectures or tasks. Choosing which layers to connect and which information to pass can require extensive manual tuning. This paper makes those choices learnable.

The proposed method trains meta-networks that decide which source and target layers should be matched. They also choose the features to transfer and how much knowledge each feature should contribute. This separates two connected decisions: where knowledge should enter the target network and what information should be delivered there. The authors introduce an efficient training scheme for learning those decisions.

Evaluations cover multiple datasets and network architectures. The automated method significantly outperforms the compared transfer-learning baselines, which specify what and where to transfer by hand. These findings support meta-learning as a way to configure detailed transfer relationships, particularly in the small-data setting that motivates the work.
icml-2019-learning-what-and-where-to-tra.tldr: Meta-networks learn which layers and features to transfer between networks, outperforming manually configured transfer in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies dynamical systems whose transition function is represented by a Gaussian process. Inference must account for uncertainty in both the hidden system states and the function that moves the system between states. Earlier approaches used expensive sampling methods or simplified the variational posterior by separating parts of that uncertainty.

The authors show experimentally that separating latent states from the transition function can produce poorly calibrated uncertainty and unnecessarily large learned noise terms. Their proposed variational method explicitly preserves dependence between state trajectories and a low-rank representation of the Gaussian process posterior. Conditioning on this representation makes it tractable to generate latent-state samples.

The resulting method improves predictive performance and yields better-calibrated estimates of the transition function. It maintains the same time and space complexity as mean-field methods. The contribution therefore addresses a specific approximation error while preserving computational scaling, showing that a richer treatment of dependence can improve both predictions and uncertainty estimates without changing those complexity classes.
icml-2019-overcoming-mean-field-approxim.tldr: Preserving dependence between latent trajectories and Gaussian process dynamics improves prediction and uncertainty calibration at mean-field computational complexity.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis aims to recover signal structure from data, but successful recovery depends on how many observations are available relative to dimensionality. Prior analysis established a critical observation threshold before learning begins. This paper extends that analysis to missing data, focusing on probabilistic PCA as a method for estimating signal structure in incomplete datasets.

The analytic result suggests that missing entries act by lowering the effective signal-to-noise ratio. This differs from interpreting missingness simply as having fewer samples. The distinction changes how the loss of information is understood: the proposed account emphasizes weaker recoverable signal relative to noise within the analyzed learning problem.

The theory predicts a phase transition in learning curves, meaning a threshold separates different regimes of signal recovery. The authors observe this behavior in both simulations and real datasets. These findings support the analysis and its interpretation of missing data, while retaining the qualified claim that reduced signal-to-noise ratio explains the effect studied.
icml-2019-phase-transition-in-pca-with-m.tldr: The analysis suggests missing data weakens PCA’s effective signal-to-noise ratio and predicts a recovery threshold observed in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper encourages coordination and communication by rewarding an agent for influencing other agents’ actions. Influence is assessed through counterfactual reasoning: the agent considers alternative actions it could have taken and estimates how those alternatives would change others’ behavior. Actions associated with larger changes receive greater intrinsic reward.

The authors show that this reward is equivalent to encouraging high mutual information between agents’ actions. This connects the behavioral idea of influence to a statistical relationship between their choices. They also describe a decentralized implementation in which each agent learns a neural model of other agents and uses it to compute influence rewards.

Experiments in challenging social-dilemma environments show enhanced coordination and communication, substantial improvements in learning curves, and more meaningful learned communication protocols. The decentralized implementation is consequential because earlier communication approaches discussed in the paper relied on centralized training to learn diverse policies. The findings support influence-based motivation as a shared mechanism for learning both coordinated behavior and useful communication.
icml-2019-social-influence-as-intrinsic-.tldr: Rewarding counterfactual influence over other agents improves coordination and communication and can be implemented through decentralized agent models.

paragraphs: A fair classifier can still be unstable if changes in its training data produce substantial changes in the learned model. Motivated by evidence of this problem in existing fair-classification algorithms, the paper studies how to obtain fairness and stability together. The focus is on methods expressed as optimization problems.

The proposed framework adds a regularization term specifically aimed at stability. The authors prove an additional stability guarantee and provide an accuracy guarantee for the extended framework. The accuracy result can guide the choice of regularization strength, connecting the theoretical analysis to the practical decision of how strongly to encourage stability during training.

The empirical study extends several fair-classification methods with strong fairness-accuracy balance on the Adult dataset. The modified versions improve stability with only a slight loss of accuracy in those experiments. This shows that stability can be incorporated into existing optimization-based fair-learning methods and evaluated alongside their predictive performance, rather than assuming that a favorable fairness-accuracy balance already ensures robustness to training-set variation.
icml-2019-stable-and-fair-classification.tldr: Stability-focused regularization adds guarantees to fair classifiers and improves empirical stability with a slight accuracy cost.

paragraphs: Density estimation seeks a model of how probability is distributed across possible observations. This paper develops a framework for high-dimensional density estimation using triangular maps, which provide transformations between source and target probability densities. The framework specifies one-dimensional transformations, equivalently conditional densities, together with networks that condition those transformations.

This common description brings autoregressive and flow-based approaches into the same analytical framework. It exposes their shared structure, differences, representational capabilities, and limitations. The authors use that perspective to develop a Sum-of-Squares polynomial flow, describing the resulting model as interpretable, universal in representation, and easy to train.

Synthetic experiments examine transformations across different density geometries, illustrating both benefits and shortcomings. Additional evaluations on simulations and real-world datasets show competitive results for SOS flows. The paper’s contribution therefore has two connected parts: a framework for understanding existing density models and a new model motivated by that framework. Its representational claims and empirical competitiveness address different aspects of the proposed approach.
icml-2019-sum-of-squares-polynomial-flow.tldr: A triangular-map framework unifies density-estimation approaches and motivates an interpretable, universal Sum-of-Squares polynomial flow.

paragraphs: Larger convolutional neural networks often achieve better accuracy, but increasing parameter counts may conflict with resource constraints. This paper asks how to improve the capacity of a CNN with large-scale features while keeping its parameter budget fixed. Its approach changes how a convolutional layer allocates its existing resources.

The proposed layer learns channel selectivity: it selects important channels and redistributes their parameters. This introduces a learned allocation decision within a standard convolutional layer. The goal is to make the available parameters more useful, so that model improvement can come from how resources are assigned as well as from how many parameters exist.

Experiments across multiple CNN architectures and datasets show that the modified layer reaches solutions that generalize better than the baseline. The authors attribute this improvement to efficient resource use and access to new optima during training. The evidence supports channel selection and parameter redistribution as a way to improve the evaluated networks without adding parameters to obtain those gains.
icml-2019-training-cnns-with-selective-a.tldr: A channel-selective convolutional layer reallocates existing parameters and improves generalization in the evaluated CNNs without increasing parameter count.

paragraphs: Strong visual representations often depend on extensive manual labeling, which can restrict where deep image models are practical. This paper proposes training without manual label supervision by progressively discovering neighborhoods of examples around individual samples. These neighborhoods supply a structure from which the model can learn distinctions between unseen classes.

Each neighborhood is constructed so that its members have a high probability of sharing the same unknown class label. The method uses these groups to develop class-discriminative features and iteratively reason about class decision boundaries. Discovery and learning accumulate over time, allowing the training process to build on the neighborhoods it has identified.

Experiments on six image-classification benchmarks show advantages over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods. The benchmarks include both broad object categories and finer distinctions within categories. These results support neighborhood discovery as a source of supervision for visual feature learning. The approach relies on probable shared labels within groups; the abstract does not claim that every discovered neighborhood has perfectly uniform class membership.
icml-2019-unsupervised-deep-learning-by-.tldr: Progressively discovering likely same-class neighborhoods trains discriminative visual features without manual labels and improves results on six benchmarks.
